Component exported as `TwoFactor` in BackupCode.tsx

The default export in `BackupCode.tsx` is named `TwoFactor` (copy-paste from the TOTP component). This misleads readers and shows up as `TwoFactor` in React DevTools/stack traces for two different components. Rename to `BackupCode`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the inconsistent naming of the exported TwoFactor component in BackupCode.tsx, which handles backup codes rather than TOTP.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a read-modify-write race

The backup code is validated and then invalidated via a separate `prisma.user.update` using the decrypted array read earlier. Two concurrent login attempts with the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either write lands, so a single backup code can be redeemed more than once (and the second write can also resurrect codes nulled by the first, since the whole array is re-serialized from stale data). Use an atomic conditional update or a transaction with row locking so each code can only be consumed once.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same read-modify-write race: concurrent login requests can validate the same backup code before either update completes, allowing a supposedly one-time code to be accepted more than once.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
backupCodes state typed as never[] and blob URL never revoked

`useState([])` infers `never[]`, so `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` and `backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` only type-check because the response body is `any`; any future typing of the response will break. Additionally the object URL created with `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked when a new one is created — it is never revoked when the modal unmounts, leaking the blob (containing the plaintext backup codes) for the lifetime of the document.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the backup-code object URL is not revoked when the modal unmounts, causing a blob memory leak. This matches the golden issue despite the additional state-typing concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes are overwritten on every setup call and can never be regenerated afterwards

`/totp/setup` unconditionally regenerates and stores new `backupCodes`, and `/totp/disable` nulls them. There is no endpoint or UI to view or regenerate codes once 2FA is enabled. Consequently, if the user closes the "Backup Codes" dialog (e.g. via the dialog X / `onOpenChange`) without copying or downloading, the codes are permanently unrecoverable while 2FA stays enabled, leaving the user with no recovery path. A regenerate endpoint (or showing codes again from settings) is needed.

Download button is nested in an anchor inside a form without type="button"

The download `Button` is rendered inside an `<a download>` which itself is inside the `<Form>` for `handleEnable`, and the button sets no `type` and no `preventDefault`. If the shared Button does not default to `type="button"`, clicking Download will also submit the enable form (re-running `handleEnable` with an empty totpCode) and may interrupt the download. Add `type="button"` explicitly, as done for the copy/close buttons via `preventDefault`.

No test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The new authentication path (backup code verification in `next-auth-options.ts` and in `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable`) including single-use invalidation is untested; the test only clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen (with TODOs for content). A regression that accepts an invalid code, fails to invalidate a used code, or breaks the backup-code login screen would not be caught.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Destructuring an empty destinationCalendar array causes TypeError

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` can yield `undefined`, and the next line dereferences it unguarded: `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`. For any booking with Google Meet as location and no destination calendar (now commonly `[]` or `null`, e.g. handleCancelBooking and the stripe/paypal webhooks pass `[]`), `EventManager.create` throws `Cannot read properties of undefined`, breaking booking creation. Use optional chaining.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: destructuring a null or empty destinationCalendar produces an undefined mainHostDestinationCalendar, which is then dereferenced without a guard. The candidate's different attribution to EventManager.create and omission of updateEvent do not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback lookup is always undefined

`const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — the `find` branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it compares each `cal.externalId` against `undefined` and can never match. The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Result: when no externalCalendarId is stored on the reference, `calendarId` becomes undefined and the Google update/delete targets the wrong (default) calendar or fails. The same pattern exists in `deleteEvent` (line 317), where it then silently falls back to `primary`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same faulty destination-calendar lookup comparing cal.externalId to externalCalendarId. The candidate more precisely explains that the lookup runs only when externalCalendarId is falsy, causing the fallback calendar lookup to fail.

false_positives.candidate:
externalId not recorded for destinations without credentialId

In the `else` branch (destination without `credentialId`), `createEvent(c, event)` is called without the third `externalId` argument, so `EventResult.externalId` is undefined and the booking reference gets `externalCalendarId: undefined` (line 169 now derives it from `result.externalId` instead of `evt.destinationCalendar.externalId`). Subsequent updates/cancellations then cannot locate the event in the right calendar.

Possible duplicate event creation for *_other_calendar destinations

After the destination loop, all credentials whose type includes `other_calendar` are unconditionally used to create another event. If a destinationCalendar entry points to one of those credentials (its `credentialId` matches, or its `integration` equals the credential type), the event is created twice for that integration, producing duplicate calendar entries and duplicate booking references.

Team destination calendars dropped when evt.destinationCalendar is null

`evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op when `destinationCalendar` is `null` (which happens when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar). In a collective event where only the non-organizer hosts have calendars connected, their calendars are silently ignored — exactly the case this PR aims to fix. Initialize to `[]` and push instead.

Dynamic booking user select lost `organization.slug`

The rewritten `loadUsers` drops `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the dynamic (no eventTypeId) user query that the previous code selected. Any downstream code relying on `user.organization?.slug` (e.g. booker/organizer URL construction for org users) will now see it missing for dynamic group bookings.

BOOKING_CREATED/BOOKING_REQUESTED webhook assertions not updated for array payload

Only the BOOKING_REJECTED expectation was changed to `destinationCalendar: []`. The BOOKING_CREATED (line 119) and BOOKING_REQUESTED (line 373) expectations still assert `destinationCalendar: null`, but `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` is now an array (`[]` or a list). These assertions will fail or, worse, pass accidentally and no longer verify the payload shape.

Legacy-reference cancellation path now deletes once per reference per credential

The loop over all `_calendar` references combined with the inner `else` branch (iterating every user calendar credential) means for N legacy references with M calendar credentials, M*N delete calls are issued, each using that reference's `uid`/`externalCalendarId` against unrelated credentials. This multiplies API calls and generates spurious 404s compared to the previous single-reference behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach with async callback escapes the surrounding try/catch and is not awaited

Changing the callback to `async` means `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` fires off floating promises: the enclosing try/catch can no longer catch errors from `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` (they become unhandled rejections), and the function returns/sends the reschedule email before the calendar/video events are deleted. Replace with `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered) { await ... }` or `await Promise.all(map(...))`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify async callbacks passed to forEach as unawaited fire-and-forget operations, causing unhandled rejections, ineffective surrounding try/catch, and premature completion of cleanup. Both recommend for...of with await or Promise.all with map.

false_positives.candidate:
appStore map invokes import() eagerly, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded

Each property is initialized with `import("./app")` evaluated at module-evaluation time, so importing `@calcom/app-store` immediately starts loading every app package (and bundlers will include them all in the graph). The only change versus the previous static imports is that consumers must now `await`; there is no deferral and no bundle-size/cold-start win. To get the intended async behaviour the values must be thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) resolved on demand.

Eagerly created import promises can produce unhandled rejections

Because all ~28 dynamic import promises are created at module load, a failure in any single app module (missing dependency, throwing top-level code) results in a rejected promise that nobody awaits unless that specific app is used. In Node this surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection and can terminate the process, even for apps the request never touches. Deferring the import until the app is requested avoids this.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in the `calendar` field, breaking external consumers

`getCalendar` is now async, so `getCalendarCredentials()[n].calendar` is a `Promise<Calendar | null>` rather than `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated (it awaits `item.calendar`). Any other caller of `getCalendarCredentials` that uses `.calendar` directly (e.g. API/trpc handlers for connected calendars, availability code) will now silently operate on a Promise object, producing runtime errors or truthy-but-useless values. All call sites need auditing/updating.

forEach with async callback escapes the surrounding try/catch and is not awaited

Same problem as the vital variant: the async callback passed to `forEach` is not awaited, so errors from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent` and `deleteMeeting` bypass the enclosing try/catch (becoming unhandled rejections) and cancellation of the external calendar/video events may not have happened by the time the function returns true and the email is sent.

requestReschedule fires un-awaited async forEach for calendar/video deletion

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { await getCalendar(...) ... })` creates floating promises. The mutation continues to send the reschedule email and webhooks and returns to the client while the deleteEvent/deleteMeeting calls may still be pending, and any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no logging. Await the deletions (for...of or Promise.all) before proceeding.

Commented example path is wrong

The placeholder comment reads `// example: import("./example")`, but the example app lives in `_example` (the previous code commented `import * as example from "./_example"`). Anyone uncommenting it will get a module-not-found error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag name "shards" vs "shard"

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `shards=` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `shard=`. This breaks dashboards/queries grouping on a single tag key. Also note the tag value is now a comma-joined list of shards, which changes cardinality and the meaning of existing `shard` tags on these metrics.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same metric tag inconsistency: wait_produce uses 'shards' while produce and segment_size_bytes use 'shard', preventing consistent aggregation/dashboards. The candidate's extra note about comma-joined values does not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep is monkeypatched to a no-op, so the added sleep does not wait

`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the test makes the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (and its comment about giving flusher threads time) a no-op. The test therefore still races against the flusher thread producing into `messages`, and the following `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. Use a real wait/poll loop (e.g. a saved reference to the original sleep or polling until messages is non-empty).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in test_basic: time.sleep is monkeypatched to a no-op, so the subsequent time.sleep(0.1) does not actually wait and the test can race the flusher thread.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhealthy spawn processes are never killed due to isinstance check

In `_ensure_processes_alive` the kill is now guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which produces a `SpawnProcess` that derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process` (the default-context class). The guard therefore evaluates False and hung flusher processes are never killed before a replacement is started, leaking processes that still hold Redis connections and keep flushing the same shards concurrently with the new process (duplicate/fragmented segment production). The same problem applies to `process.terminate()` in `join()` (line 346). Use `BaseProcess` or check for `threading.Thread` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: flusher processes created via get_context('spawn').Process are SpawnProcess instances not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process, so the isinstance guard is always false and hung processes are never killed. The candidate adds extra detail about consequences and join(), but the core issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep is monkeypatched to a no-op, so the added sleep does not wait

`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the test makes the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (and its comment about giving flusher threads time) a no-op. The test therefore still races against the flusher thread producing into `messages`, and the following `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. Use a real wait/poll loop (e.g. a saved reference to the original sleep or polling until messages is non-empty).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that monkeypatched time.sleep makes the test's sleep a no-op, so it doesn't wait for the flusher and can race; the candidate just adds a suggested fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of shutdown loop leaving remaining processes untouched

In `join()`, when the deadline is exceeded the loop `break`s, so processes with higher indices are never waited on nor terminated. With multiple flusher processes, a timed-out shutdown can leave daemon processes alive that continue flushing segments while the consumer rebalances. `remaining_time` is also computed but unused. Terminate all processes unconditionally after the wait loop instead of breaking out.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same shutdown bug: breaking out of the join loop when the deadline elapses skips waiting on/terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running. The candidate's suggested fix aligns with the golden concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead/incorrect helper `_create_process_for_shard`

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is never called anywhere after the refactor (health checking now restarts by process index). Dead code that duplicates restart logic and has no restart-counter accounting; it should be removed to avoid future misuse that bypasses the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS guard.

Multi-process flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, not behaviour

`test_flusher_processes_limit` checks `len(flusher.processes)`, `max_processes` and the shard count, but never submits spans nor verifies that segments from all 4 shards are actually flushed by the 2 workers. The core new behaviour (shard partitioning across processes, per-process backpressure/health, no duplicate or missing segments) is untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs error ids with node values by position

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict whose value ordering matches the order of `error_ids`. That is an implementation detail of the backend (and of how it builds its result dict); if the ordering differs, each `ErrorEvent.id` will be attached to a different event's title/message/timestamp, producing silently wrong summaries. Index by node id instead: build `node_id -> error_id` and look up `events[node_id]`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: zip(error_ids, events.values()) relies on get_multi preserving input order, but dict value order is not guaranteed, so events can be paired with the wrong error IDs. The candidate's suggested node-id lookup addresses that same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Flagged TableWidgetVisualization branch renders a hard-coded empty table

When the organization has the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature, the table branch renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of passing the actual `result`/`fields`/`result.meta`. Any org with the flag enabled will see completely blank table widgets (no headers, no rows) rather than their data. The real query results must be mapped into `TabularData`/`TabularColumn` before this can be enabled.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded empty columns/data instead of actual query results, so enabled orgs see blank tables.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
age/timestamp mutual-exclusion checks use truthiness

`validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")` for truthiness. A report with `age: 0` (very common — a report generated just now) plus a `timestamp` will not be flagged, and `timestamp: 0` likewise. Use `is not None` / `in self.initial_data`. Also, neither field is required, so a report with neither `age` nor `timestamp` passes validation entirely.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same mutual-exclusion bug: truthiness checks on .get('age') and .get('timestamp') incorrectly treat 0 as absent. It recommends presence checks such as 'in self.initial_data', matching the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics recorded before feature gate and schema validation

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `features.has(...)` check and before request validation, so the event is emitted even for orgs without the feature (404 responses) and for malformed requests. This inflates the metric and makes it unusable for measuring real assembles. Move the call after the feature check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: analytics.record is called before the feature flag check, so events are logged even for requests that return 404 because the feature is disabled, inflating/misleading analytics. The candidate adds schema validation as an extra concern, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Error/breadcrumb timestamps compared in different units

In `gen_request_data`, error timestamps come from nodestore event data (`data.get("timestamp")`, seconds since epoch) while rrweb replay events use millisecond epoch timestamps. The merge loop compares `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)` directly, so every error will always compare as earlier than every replay event and all error log lines will be emitted before any breadcrumb, destroying the chronological interleaving the function is meant to produce. One side needs unit normalization.

get_environment_info fetches a recommended event per issue

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` and then `get_environment()` for each of the up-to-5 issues while building a PR comment. Each call is an additional snuba/nodestore + DB round trip inside a task that previously only used fields already loaded on the Group. This noticeably increases latency/cost for every merged-PR comment; consider batching or caching the environment lookup.

One invalid report rejects an entire browser report batch

Browsers send batches of reports to the Reporting API endpoint. The new loop returns 422 as soon as any single report fails validation, discarding the valid reports in the same request. Since the browser will retry the whole batch, one malformed/unknown report type permanently blocks collection of the others. Prefer validating per report and skipping (with a metric/log) the invalid ones while returning 200.

useTraceItemAttributeKeys can now return undefined attributes

Previously `attributes` was always a `TagCollection` (built with `useMemo` from `result.data ?? []`). It is now `isFetching ? previous : data`, where both `previous` and `data` can be `undefined` (first load, or when `enabled` is false / query errors). Callers doing `Object.keys(attributes)` or spreading it will throw at runtime. Default to `{}` or update the return type and all consumers.

dcg_to_slow_conditions now keyed only by dcg_ids, risking KeyError

`get_condition_query_groups` previously computed slow conditions from `event_data.dcg_to_groups.keys()`, and `get_groups_to_fire` from `event_data.dcg_ids`. Both now receive a single map built from `event_data.dcg_ids`, and both still index it with `dcg_to_slow_conditions[dcg.id]`. If `dcg_to_groups` contains any group id not present in `dcg_ids` (or `get_slow_conditions_for_groups` omits ids with no slow conditions rather than returning a defaultdict), this raises KeyError and the whole delayed-workflow batch fails. Use `.get(dcg.id, [])` or assert the key sets are identical.

Comment points at a migration that does not exist in this change

Both 0917 and 0920 now say "See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration", but no 0921 migration is added in this PR. Readers (and anyone auditing why the data migration was neutered) will look for a file that isn't there; either land the replacement migration in the same change or reword the comment.

enabled guard `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always true

`normalizeDateTimeParams` returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is unconditionally `true` and contributes nothing to the `enabled` condition. If the intent was to wait until page filters are ready, check `usePageFilters().isReady` or a specific field instead; as written the query may fire with default/unready filters.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage on groups to admins holding only the view scope

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` evaluates `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it returns true if the caller only has the `view` scope on the `Groups` resource type. `canManage()` backs `requireManage()` used by `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup`, so an admin granted only all-groups `view` can create top-level groups. The scope list should contain only `MANAGE` (compare `canManage(GroupModel)` at line 79, which correctly uses only `MANAGE`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(): the permission check includes VIEW as well as MANAGE, so view-only admins incorrectly pass the manage check and gain write access. The candidate's wording and example (addTopLevelGroup) describe the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs instead of group IDs

In V2, the authz resource created for a group is named with the group id (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`, which returns `group.getId()` as the resource name), while `resource.getId()` is an unrelated resource UUID. `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set, and that set is stored as the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute in `UsersResource.searchForUser`/`BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser` and passed to `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`. With wrong ids, the store-level filtering/count matches no groups, so user counts are reported as 0 and group-scoped user queries return nothing. Use `groupResource.getName()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: it returns authz resource UUIDs (resource.getId()) rather than the underlying group IDs, which are stored as the resource name. During re-authentication (user already set in context) the passkey/WebAuthn form elements will therefore be rendered even for users who have no passkey registered, offering an authentication option that cannot succeed. true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative slice start on a QuerySet raises ValueError

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, `start_offset` is negative and `queryset[start_offset:stop]` is evaluated. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indexing (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so a client-supplied negative cursor offset produces an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. The comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in OptimizedCursorPaginator: negative cursor offsets produce negative queryset slices, which Django does not support, causing an unhandled error. The exception type differs (AssertionError vs ValueError), but the underlying issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member can be None -> AttributeError

For a superuser or staff user who is not a member of the organization, `organization_context.member` is None, so `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises AttributeError and returns a 500. Because Python evaluates `or` left-to-right the superuser case short-circuits, but any non-member non-superuser request reaching this line (e.g. via org-level permission grants or token auth where member is None) crashes. Guard with `organization_context.member and ...`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: organization_context.member may be None for token/org-auth requests, so accessing has_global_access raises AttributeError. The candidate's broader examples don't change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the datetime sort key

The endpoint orders by `-datetime` and uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `math.floor(getattr(item, 'datetime'))` and whose `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value. `math.floor()` on a `datetime` raises TypeError, and the raw int cursor value cannot be compared against a datetime column in `build_queryset`. Any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an eligible user will 500 (or produce a bad SQL comparison). A DateTimePaginator-style key conversion is required.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator is used with a datetime sort key (-datetime) but get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil and value_from_cursor returns a raw numeric cursor, which will TypeError or produce an invalid comparison.

false_positives.candidate:
has_global_access used as admin authorization gate

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` treats any member with global/open-membership access as an "authorized administrator" and unlocks the OptimizedCursorPaginator's unchecked negative-offset path. `has_global_access` only means the member can see all teams in the org; it is not an admin/privilege flag. This grants ordinary members a non-standard pagination code path that deliberately bypasses offset bounds checks. The gate should be an explicit permission check (or the feature removed).

Silently clamping offset hides invalid cursors and breaks drop-extra logic

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently clamps a negative forward offset to 0 instead of surfacing an error, so a malformed/attacker-supplied cursor now returns page 1 data rather than being rejected. Worse, the subsequent check at line 192 still uses the unclamped `offset` (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`), so when offset is clamped the extra-row trimming comparison is computed against a different window size than was fetched, producing wrong has-more/trimming behavior. For `is_prev` the negative offset is still passed through to the slice and will raise ValueError from Django.

Duplicate trimming logic uses unclamped offset

`elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` in OptimizedCursorPaginator compares the result count against a window computed from the raw `cursor.offset`, while the slice actually used `start_offset` (clamped, or negative). When these differ the extra prev-row is not dropped (or is dropped incorrectly), yielding duplicated/missing rows across pages. This whole method is a copy-paste of BasePaginator.get_result and should delegate instead of duplicating the logic.

No tests for new OptimizedCursorPaginator or clamping behavior

A new public paginator class plus a behavioral change to BasePaginator.get_result offset handling are added with no accompanying tests. There is no coverage for negative offsets, the clamping branch, or the new endpoint query parameter, so the ValueError/TypeError crashes described above would not be caught by CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its whole body, which serialized index creation. Now only the cache write is locked, so two callers for the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event handler plus startup build, or two concurrent search requests that both see a nil index via GetIndex) can run bleve.New() against the same on-disk directory concurrently. bleve.New fails or corrupts state when the directory already exists/is open, and the second winner overwrites the cache entry while the first index is still referenced by a caller. Some per-key coordination (e.g. a keyed mutex / singleflight) is needed, not just a cache-write lock.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition in BuildIndex: moving b.cacheMu from protecting the entire function to only the final cache write allows concurrent goroutines to build the same index key, requiring per-key coordination.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex now writes to the map under cacheMu from worker goroutines and from the watch-event path. Concurrent map read/write panics the process. This is newly reachable because search.init() now logs s.search.TotalDocs() and index builds can be triggered asynchronously by the watch goroutine. Take cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache unsynchronized while BuildIndex writes the map under cacheMu, now reachable via the new TotalDocs call and async watch-triggered index builds, risking a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background resources

When s.Init(ctx) returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel() on the context created above (and without stopping any lifecycle/blob resources already initialized). The context and any goroutines started during partial init (e.g. the storage watch poller started by backend WatchWriteEvents) are leaked for the life of the process. Call cancel() (and ideally s.Stop) before returning the error.

Shared `err` variable written from concurrent errgroup goroutines

Inside the `for _, info := range stats` loop, each goroutine assigns to the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and also increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` counter without synchronization. With initWorkers > 1 these are concurrent writes to the same variables — a data race that can be detected by -race and can mask or mis-report build errors (one goroutine's error being overwritten by another's nil). Use a goroutine-local `err :=` and an atomic counter.

Since this PR changes initialization to happen eagerly at ResourceServer construction (the riskiest behavioral change here), the test that would catch startup regressions no longer runs on postgres in CI, leaving that configuration uncovered.

false_positives.candidate:
queue_pool is created once per factory but destroyed on strategy close, breaking processing after a rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is constructed once in `__init__` and reused by every `create_with_partitions` call. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which permanently stops the worker threads and shuts down the queues. Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again after every partition revoke/assign (rebalance), so the second strategy will be handed a pool whose workers are dead and whose queues raise `ShutDown` on put. From then on the consumer silently accepts messages that are never processed and never commits, i.e. it stalls permanently until the process is restarted. The pool needs to be created per strategy (or recreated when it has been shut down).

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)` (ultimately arroyo's `commit` passed to `create_with_partitions`). Arroyo's commit callback and the underlying Kafka consumer are not thread-safe and are expected to be called from the strategy/processing thread (the same thread that calls `poll`/`submit`). Calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor's own consumer operations can corrupt consumer state or crash librdkafka. Offsets should instead be accumulated and committed from `poll()`.

No final commit on close(), and offset state survives rebalances

`close()` sets `shutdown_event` (ending `_commit_loop` without a last pass) and then shuts the pool down after workers drain remaining queued items. Offsets for everything processed since the last 1-second tick, plus everything drained during shutdown, are therefore never committed, so those messages are reprocessed after restart. Additionally `OffsetTracker` state (`all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed`) is never reset on partition revocation; because the pool/tracker is shared across `create_with_partitions` calls, a new strategy can commit offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns. A final `get_committable_offsets()`/commit after draining, plus per-assignment tracker reset, is needed.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite docstring claim

`queue.Queue()` is created with no maxsize and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but in practice a slow group can accumulate unbounded work items (each holding the decoded result and the original Kafka `Message`), growing memory without limit and making the uncommitted offset window unbounded. Set a maxsize and raise `MessageRejected` when full so arroyo throttles consumption.

Decode/submit failures are silently acked instead of DLQ'd

In `submit`, any exception (including the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` and the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` inside `decode_payload`) is swallowed and the offset is immediately marked added+complete, so the message is committed as if processed. This drops messages without routing them to the DLQ and will also silently discard every `FilteredPayload` while logging an exception for each. Filtered payloads should be handled explicitly and genuine failures should be surfaced/DLQ'd rather than acked.

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were added in Python 3.13. On an older interpreter the module-level reference raises `AttributeError` at worker runtime and `q.shutdown()` is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, leaving workers blocked forever in `work_queue.get()` and making shutdown hang for 5s per worker. If the project must support <3.13, use a sentinel item to stop workers instead.

Transaction name hardcodes "monitors" prefix for generic remote-subscription consumer

The sentry_sdk transaction is named `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this strategy is generic to remote subscriptions (uptime being the first user). Uptime traffic will be reported under a `monitors.*` transaction name, making performance data misleading.

OptimizedCursorPaginator allows negative offsets, enabling unbounded/invalid queryset slicing

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError/AssertionError` ("Negative indexing is not supported"), so any user-supplied cursor with a negative offset on the audit-log endpoint causes a 500. The inline comments claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" are factually wrong. There is also no validation rejecting negative offsets as other paginators do (`BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset path (enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0) passes the negative offset directly into queryset slicing, which Django does not support.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

BasePaginator offset clamping changes pagination behavior inconsistently

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` clamps forward offsets to 0 but leaves prev-cursor offsets unclamped, so a negative offset on a prev cursor still reaches the queryset slice and crashes. Additionally the later check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` still uses the unclamped `offset`, so when clamping occurred the extra-row trimming is computed against the wrong expected length and an extra row may be returned on a page.

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally; `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for users who are not members of the organization (e.g. a superuser accessing another org), which raises `AttributeError` and returns a 500 for every GET request in that case. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same AttributeError risk from unconditionally accessing organization_context.member.has_global_access when the member context is absent. The candidate adds an authentication caveat, but the core deduplication concern matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Undocumented query flag switches paginator and breaks cursor semantics for audit logs

`optimized_pagination=true` swaps `DateTimePaginator` for `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor` treat the ordering key as a numeric value, not a datetime. Ordering is by `-datetime`, so `int(math.floor(value))` on a `datetime` raises `TypeError`, and cursors issued by one paginator are not interpretable by the other. This path appears untested and will 500 as soon as it is exercised.

Span eviction limit hardcoded to 1000 and silently drops spans, ignoring max_segment_spans config

The eviction threshold `1000` is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is now unused in Python, so the configured limit has no effect and the two can diverge. More importantly `zpopmin` removes the spans with the lowest `end_timestamp_precise`, silently discarding span data from oversized segments without any metric/log (the previous code incremented `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and skipped the segment). Oversized segments will now be emitted partially, and the dropped span may be the root/segment span, producing a segment with the wrong `is_segment` marking.

span_count can be stale/incorrect when both unions execute

`span_count` is assigned from the first `zunionstore` and then possibly overwritten by the second, which is fine, but if only the first union runs and the parent merge is skipped, `span_count` reflects the cardinality *before* the current span's own zadd in some orderings; and if neither union runs `zcard` is queried. The net effect is that when a union happened, the count used for the `> 1000` eviction check can be lower than the actual set size (the new span payload is added by a separate pipeline step), so segments can exceed the intended cap or evict the wrong amount. Prefer always calling `zcard set_key` right before the eviction check.

Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing explanatory comment

The loop bound was lowered from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. Traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now fail to be joined into a single segment, producing split segments, and the behavioral trade-off is no longer documented anywhere.

max_segment_spans is now dead config and missing from __reduce__

The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so `max_segment_spans` is no longer used anywhere; callers configuring it get no effect. Relatedly `__reduce__` still only passes `assigned_shards`, the two timeouts and `redis_ttl`, so `segment_page_size`, `max_segment_bytes` and `max_segment_spans` are reset to defaults when the buffer is pickled for multiprocessing — any non-default tuning is silently lost in the multiprocess consumer path.

No test for the new in-insert eviction behavior

The PR's headline change (zset-based buffer with eviction of the oldest spans once a segment exceeds 1000 spans) has no test. Tests were only mechanically updated with `end_timestamp_precise`. A test asserting that a segment with >1000 spans keeps the newest 1000 (and what happens to the root span) is needed, since this path silently drops customer data if it misbehaves.

However, it emphasizes collisions/staleness rather than cross-process hash randomization specifically.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

false_positives.candidate:
Cached value type not validated; truthy-return instead of bool
